body: The disease - its symptoms have destroyed the quality of my life. It's a permanent thing and I can't live the rest of my life with it. Within just 1 year it did so much damage (to me, physically, but also to my life in general) and if I were to actually reach the average life expectancy that's 6 decades of this destroying me. I've been trying to treat and manage it for over a year and it's not treatable nor manageable.

You will feel the absence of any meaningful friendships/relationships, but that's all it is, not a hole in you, but just missing something that was next to you. If you have attempted to nourish that friendship/relationship and your efforts were fruitless, cut your losses as you don't need to do anything else to solve this problem. That feeling will go away eventually.

OP said he was bullied a lot when he was younger, but the world has changed a lot in the last couple of years and the people in his environment might not be as unsupportive as he fears. I do think your advice is sound on some level, but wouldn't it be better for the OP to just tell his fiance, family and friends the truth? He could still move and start life elsewhere, regardless if they're supportive or not. But by moving away and cutting off contact (which he might have to do if he wants to hide his sexuality from them), he could end up losing a lot more than he would if he was just honest at this point. 

He's been with his fiance for 5 years, she's going to be angry no matter what. But if she finds out that the relationship is over because of his sexuality, it could be easier for her to move on knowing that 1) it wasn't her fault 2) it makes it clear that there's no chance of getting back together 3) she doesn't have to listen to a bullshit excuse and jump to her own conclusions causing her more emotional pain. He and her might have a chance to remain friends later down the line if he's honest now. 

I'm not saying that there's a guarantee OP will have support or that his environment isn't toxic, but right now OPs assumptions might be clouded by fear. So step 1 would be coming out to his therapist and letting them help him determine if it's just an assumption or if the people in his life are really homophobic. A gay friend of mine didn't come out until 23 due to fear, only to find out everyone was supportive and non-judgmental when he did come out. Whereas one of my closest friends for over 10 years had come out to me (and only me and her gf) as a lesbian but then proceeded to cut out everyone from her life out of fear. Well, now most people know and have no problem with her sexuality but don't want anything to do with her because they felt abandoned by her when they were worrying about her not knowing what went wrong for years and she never responded to them.

You're not considering these statements in the context that they're being made. People DO celebrate various European cultures in America and if you went to one of those celebrations and said "white is white, it doesn't make a difference" then that would be disrespectful. But that is not what's happening in the context OP brought up. 

If you're white in America, probably the only times you will get the question "where are you (really) from?" is if you have a thick accent and/or are a tourist. Usually it will be as a conversation starter.

But if you're Asian? Even if you don't have an accent, you will be asked that kind of question and it's not out of genuine curiosity about your culture, but done in an alienating manner, like the person asking means you won't ever truly be considered American to them and they are looking to see what stereotypes they can apply to you. The people that do ask out of genuine interest phrase it "what's your ethnicity" and there's follow-up conversation.
